outcome: The Republic of Ghana’s independence from British colonial rule in 1957 inspired visits from African American activists such as Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, writer Maya Angelou, lawyer Pauli Murray, and historian and sociologist W.E.B. Du Bois.

topic: Topic 4.2: Anticolonialism and Black Political Thought
subtopic: Black Freedom movement in the twentieth century
outcome: In 1960, renowned boxer Joe Louis traveled with a predominantly African American delegation to Cuba to discuss plans to promote Cuba as a tourist destination for African Americans to escape the prevalence of Jim Crow discrimination and segregation.

topic: Topic 4.2: Anticolonialism and Black Political Thought
subtopic: Diasporic solidarity between African Americans and Africans impacted Black…
outcome: Explain how diasporic solidarity between African Americans and Africans impacted Black politics in the U.S. and abroad in the twentieth century and beyond.

topic: Topic 4.2: Anticolonialism and Black Political Thought
subtopic: Diasporic solidarity between African Americans and Africans impacted Black…
outcome: As African Americans and Africans acknowledged their shared struggles against anti-Black racism and oppression, diasporic solidarity between them bolstered the global reach of the Black Freedom movement to audiences beyond the United States.

topic: Topic 4.2: Anticolonialism and Black Political Thought
subtopic: Diasporic solidarity between African Americans and Africans impacted Black…
outcome: Diasporic solidarity between African Americans and Africans brought international attention to Africa’s decolonization movement. In 1960, also known as the “Year of Africa,” 17 African nations declared their independence from European colonialism. Diasporic solidarity continues to the present day.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War
outcome: Describe African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War
outcome: The United States Armed Forces remained segregated at the outset of the Second World War. Despite this, over two million African Americans registered for the draft or voluntarily enlisted and served in every branch of the United States military.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War
outcome: The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American pilots in the United States military. Serving in the United States Army Air Corps (the precursor to the United States Air Force), these pilots contributed to the fight against fascism through their service in Europe and North Africa during the Second World War.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War
outcome: Explain how the Double V Campaign emerged during the Second World War.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ involvement in the Second World War
outcome: During the era of the Second World War, African Americans critiqued the unequal treatment they faced as United States citizens as the country rallied to fight fascism in Europe. In 1942, veteran and journalist James G. Thompson inspired the “Double Victory” Campaign with a letter to the African American newspaper, Pittsburgh Courier. His letter urged readers to fight for the “double victory”—a victory against fascism abroad and a victory against Jim Crow segregation at home.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ access to the benefits of the G.I.…
outcome: Describe African Americans’ access to the benefits of the G.I. Bill.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ access to the benefits of the G.I.…
outcome: The G.I. Bill of 1944 was designed as a raceneutral gesture of gratitude toward American veterans returning from the Second World War, including 1.2 million Black veterans, by providing funds for college tuition, low-cost home mortgages, and low-interest business startup loans—major pillars of economic stability and mobility.

topic: Topic 4.3: African Americans and the Second World War: The Double V Campaign and the G.I. Bill
subtopic: African Americans’ access to the benefits of the G.I.…
outcome: Although the G.I. Bill was a federal program, funds were administered locally and subject to Jim Crow discriminatory practices. As a result, they were often disproportionately disbursed to white veterans.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life…
outcome: Describe the enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life that African Americans faced in the first half of the twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life…
outcome: Through the mid-twentieth century, African Americans in the North and South continued to face racial discrimination, violence, and segregation in education, housing, transportation, and voting. The Civil Rights movement emerged from the need to eradicate segregation and ensure federal protection of the rights guaranteed by the Reconstruction Amendments and the Civil Rights Act of 1875 (which outlawed racial discrimination in public places).

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life…
outcome: Explain the rationale for the Brown v. Board of Education decision to overturn “separate but equal.” Explain the rationale for the Brown v. Board of Education decision to overturn “separate but equal.”

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life…
outcome: In 1954, the Supreme Court ruled racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional in the Brown v. Board of Education decision. The decision determined state-sanctioned school segregation violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and overturned the prior ruling of “separate but equal” established in Plessy v. Ferguson.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Enduring forms of segregation and discrimination in daily life…
outcome: The Supreme Court cited the “doll test” conducted by psychologists Mamie and Kenneth Clark in the 1940s as a key factor in its decision: this study demonstrated the impact of racial segregation on children’s self-esteem.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Different groups responded to school integration as a result…
outcome: Explain how different groups responded to school integration as a result of the Brown v. Board of Education decision.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Different groups responded to school integration as a result…
outcome: De facto segregation in public schools persisted despite the ruling of Brown v. Board of Education. Some states cut funding for integrated schools while providing financial support to those that remained predominantly white. Some white families fled to the suburbs and private schools, shifting their investment into schools and neighborhoods that few African Americans could access. In some places, local and federal police were used to prevent integration, and some schools chose to shut down rather than integrate.

topic: Topic 4.4: Discrimination, Segregation, and the Origins of the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Different groups responded to school integration as a result…
outcome: Following the Supreme Court’s ruling in Brown v. Board of Education, students at all age levels, such as the “Little Rock Nine” (Little Rock High School, Little Rock, Arkansas, 1957), attempted to integrate schools throughout the South despite continued resistance.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: Explain the long-term effects of housing discrimination on African Americans in the second half of the twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: In the twentieth century, African Americans faced restrictions on their access to home ownership that in turn limited their ability to pass on wealth to their descendants.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: Housing segregation was codified in the Federal Housing Administration’s Underwriting Manual (1938). Restrictions made it illegal for African Americans to live in many communities in the United States. The NAACP fought housing discrimination through the passage of the Fair Housing Act in 1968.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: Throughout the twentieth century and peaking in the mid-1900s, mortgage lenders practiced redlining—the discriminatory practice of withholding mortgages to African Americans and other people of color within a defined geographical area under the pretense of “hazardous” financial risk posed by those communities.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: African Americans who integrated into wellresourced neighborhoods across the country sometimes became targets of mob violence.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: Housing discrimination intensified preexisting disparities between African Americans and white people. Many African American communities had limited access to public transportation, clean water and air, recreational spaces, healthy food, and healthcare services, exacerbating health disparities along racial lines.

topic: Topic 4.5: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
subtopic: Redlining and Housing Discrimination
outcome: Predominantly Black areas often lacked sufficient infrastructure for public transportation and racially segregated transportation remained unequal. African Americans responded by operating jitneys (small buses that provided taxi services) and starting their own bus companies.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: Describe the essential methods of the major civil rights organizations.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: Major civil rights organizations united African Americans with different experiences and perspectives through a common desire to end racial discrimination and inequality. These organizations included the “Big Four”: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: Local branches of major civil rights organizations launched a national movement built on the shared methods of nonviolent, direct, and racially inclusive protest and grassroots efforts. Nonviolent forms of civil disobedience—including marches, sit-ins, litigation, economic boycotts, and the use of mass media—were often met with violence, which sometimes precipitated a response of self-defense.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: Explain how nonviolent resistance strategies mobilized the Civil Rights movement.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: Civil rights leaders organized the Birmingham Children’s Crusade (Alabama, 1963), which strategically included children because they were not subject to penalties such as loss of homes or jobs. The violent response by local police against children was televised and met with shock and anger by many Americans and people around the world.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: In 1963, A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin, and an alliance of Black civil rights organizations and leaders from religious and labor groups organized the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. The march highlighted issues of economic inequality, unemployment, and racial discrimination. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech, calling for an end to discrimination and racism.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Essential methods of the major civil rights organizations
outcome: The Mississippi Freedom Summer project (1964) highlighted the racial violence African Americans faced while trying to assert their constitutional right to vote. The Big Four civil rights organizations established 41 Freedom Schools to prepare African Americans for civic activism through voter registration and a celebration of Black history. The killing of three young activists that summer, one African American and two Jewish, helped galvanize the movement and the formation of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Civil rights activism in the mid-twentieth century led to…
outcome: Explain how civil rights activism in the mid-twentieth century led to federal legislative achievements.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Civil rights activism in the mid-twentieth century led to…
outcome: The coordinated efforts of the Civil Rights movement resulted in the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which ended segregation and prohibited discrimination on the basis of race, color, and religion.

topic: Topic 4.6: Major Civil Rights Organizations
subtopic: Civil rights activism in the mid-twentieth century led to…
outcome: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed discriminatory barriers in voting.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: Describe the ways Black women leaders furthered the goals of the major civil rights organizations and grassroots efforts.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: Black women were central leaders in the Civil Rights movement, though they often faced gender discrimination within the major organizations. Leaders such as Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer stressed the importance of addressing both racial and gender discrimination during the Black Freedom movement, building on a long tradition of Black women activists.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: Ella Baker, known as the “mother of the Civil Rights movement,” focused on grassroots organizing and inclusive, group-centered leadership over leader-centered groups in the Civil Rights movement. She encouraged young people to contribute to social justice efforts that fought both racism and sexism.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: In her speech at SNCC’s founding in 1960, Ella Baker argued that peaceful sit-ins at lunch counters were about more than access to goods and services; they demonstrated the need for the full inclusion of African Americans in every aspect of American life.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: Dorothy Height led the National Council of Negro Women for 40 years and routinely worked on major civil rights projects, such as the March on Washington.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: Describe the ways grassroots organizing beyond the South advanced the goals of the Civil Rights movement.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: In the mid-1960s, the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO) was established to protest school segregation in Chicago. Before disbanding in 1967, it turned its attention to other issues like employment and housing discrimination plaguing Black Chicagoans.

topic: Topic 4.7: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
subtopic: Black Women’s Leadership and Grassroots Organizing in the Civil Rights Movement
outcome: In 1964, 464,000 students—nearly half of New York City’s student body—boycotted school to protest racial segregation in schools. The New York City school boycott of 1964 was the largest single-day civil rights protest in United States history.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Explain how artists, performers, poets, and musicians of African descent advocated for racial equality and brought international attention to the Black Freedom movement.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: During the Black Freedom movement of the twentieth century, Black artists contributed to the struggle for racial equality through various forms of expression. Their work brought African Americans’ resistance to inequality to global audiences and strengthened similar efforts by Afro-descendants outside of the United States.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: In their writings, poets such as Nicolás Guillén, a prominent Negrismo Cuban poet of African descent, examined the connections between anti-Black racism in the United States and Latin America. They denounced segregation and racial violence and brought Black-freedom struggles to the attention of audiences beyond the United States.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Musicians, such as jazz bassist Charles Mingus, composed protest songs reliant on African American musical traditions like call and response. Their music drew global attention to white supremacist responses to racial integration in the United States (e.g., the Little Rock Crisis, 1957).

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Explain how faith and music inspired African Americans to combat continued discrimination during the Civil Rights movement.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Faith and music were important elements of inspiration and community mobilization during the Civil Rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s. Many freedom songs emerged through the adaptation of hymns, spirituals, gospel songs, and labor union songs in Black churches, which had created space for organizing and adapting this broad range of musical genres.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Freedom songs inspired African Americans, many of whom risked their lives as they pressed for equality and freedom. These songs unified and renewed activists’ spirits, gave direction through lyrics, and communicated their hopes for a more just and inclusive future.

topic: Topic 4.8: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
subtopic: The Arts, Music, and Politics of Freedom
outcome: Martin Luther King Jr. described “We Shall Overcome” as an anthem of the Civil Rights movement. Activists often sang the song while marching, while protesting, when they were arrested, and while in jail. Exemplifying the role of freedom songs as an inspiration for political protest, the anthem served as a muse for King’s 1966 speech of the same name.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Describe the origins and beliefs of the Nation of Islam.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: The Nation of Islam (NOI) was founded in Detroit in 1930, blending basic beliefs and practices of Islam (devotion to Allah, study of the Qur’an) with mythology and Black Nationalist ideology.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Elijah Muhammad, who from 1934 led the Nation of Islam from its Chicago headquarters, encouraged his followers to forgo their surnames for Muslim ones. Many members adopted the letter “X” as a symbolic gesture of abandoning the name of their enslavers until devout members received a new identity.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Explain how Black Freedom movement strategies transitioned from civil rights to Black Power.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: During the mid-1960s, some African Americans believed the Civil Rights movement’s focus on racial integration, equal rights, and nonviolent strategies did not sufficiently address the widespread disempowerment and lack of safety they faced in their daily lives. Many embraced Black Power, a movement that promoted self-determination, defended violence as a viable strategy, and strove to transform Black consciousness by emphasizing cultural pride.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Malcolm X, a Muslim minister and activist, championed the principles of Black autonomy and encouraged African Americans to build their own social, economic, and political institutions instead of prioritizing integration.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Malcolm X not only encouraged African Americans to exercise their right to vote, but also to exercise the Second Amendment’s right to keep and bear arms. He further urged African Americans to “defend themselves” if the government was “unwilling or unable to defend the lives and the property” of African Americans. His emphasis on self-defense, dignity, and solidarity influenced the political groups that emerged during the Black Power movement.

topic: Topic 4.9: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
subtopic: Black Religious Nationalism and the Black Power Movement
outcome: Malcolm X’s ideas evolved over his lifetime. Toward the end of his life, Malcolm X left the Nation of Islam to embrace orthodox Islam. He pursued goals of Black nationalism, pan-African connections, asserting African people’s rights as human rights, and protesting injustices internationally.

topic: Topic 4.10: The Black Arts Movement
subtopic: The Black Arts Movement
outcome: Explain how the Black Arts movement (BAM) influenced Black culture in the 1960s and 1970s.

topic: Topic 4.10: The Black Arts Movement
subtopic: The Black Arts Movement
outcome: The Black Arts movement (BAM) (1965–1975) galvanized the work of Black artists, writers, musicians, and dramatists who envisioned art as a political tool to achieve Black liberation. They did not espouse a monolithic vision of what Black art should be, though they were unified by the notion that Black art was distinct in its inspiration, characteristics, and purposes.

topic: Topic 4.10: The Black Arts Movement
subtopic: The Black Arts Movement
outcome: Like the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s, which proclaimed a new mentality for the “new negro,” the Black Arts movement created a new political foundation for Black art. It emphasized the long tradition of Black cultural production by connecting contemporary writers and artists to their forerunners.

topic: Topic 4.10: The Black Arts Movement
subtopic: The Black Arts Movement
outcome: Explain how the Black Arts movement influenced the development of African American Studies.

topic: Topic 4.10: The Black Arts Movement
subtopic: The Black Arts Movement
outcome: The Black Arts movement inspired the creation of Black magazines, publishing houses, art houses, scholarly journals, and some of the earliest African American Studies programs in universities. The flourishing of Black cultural forms during this movement helped to establish African American Studies as an interdisciplinary field.

topic: Topic 4.11: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
subtopic: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
outcome: Explain how the Black Panther Party pursued political, economic, and social reforms in the twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.11: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
subtopic: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
outcome: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense was a revolutionary Black Power organization inspired by Malcolm X’s arguments. The party’s Ten-Point Program called for freedom from oppression and imprisonment, access to housing, healthcare, education, and employment opportunities.

topic: Topic 4.11: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
subtopic: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
outcome: The Black Panthers’ platform cited the Second Amendment to promote and justify the right to bear arms in self-defense. The party’s calls for violent resistance to oppression resulted in armed conflicts. In turn, the FBI waged a campaign against the Black Panthers as a threat to national security.

topic: Topic 4.11: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
subtopic: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense
outcome: Local Black Panther offices were frequently led by women, who made up about half of the party’s membership. The organization quickly expanded, with chapters in dozens of United States cities, to advocate for other social reforms. The Black Panther Party implemented what they termed “survival programs” to provide help for low-income communities: the Free Breakfast for School Children Program, legal aid offices, and relief programs that offered free medical care and clothing.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: Emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity…
outcome: Describe the emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity in the midtwentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: Emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity…
outcome: The Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity emerged in the 1960s and 1970s, respectively. Both movements emerged as African Americans embraced Black beauty and well-being and sought to strengthen their connections to Africa. They rejected notions of inferiority and conformity to mainstream standards of beauty.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: Emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity…
outcome: Explain how the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity influenced Black culture in the 1960s, 1970s, and beyond.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: Emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity…
outcome: The Black is Beautiful movement celebrated Afrocentric aesthetics in natural hairstyles (e.g., the afro and cornrows), fashion (e.g., dashikis and African head wraps), African and Islamic naming practices, celebrations like Kwanzaa (established in 1966), and the embrace of the Akan adinkra symbols like the Sankofa bird.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: Emergence of the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity…
outcome: Afrocentricity is an approach that highlights the experiences, perspectives, and aesthetics of Black people by placing Africa and the achievements of people of African descent at the center of history. This approach emerged alongside the movements in the 1960s to establish the field of African American Studies and to celebrate pride in African heritage.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: The Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity influenced the…
outcome: Explain how the Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity influenced the development of African American Studies and ethnic studies.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: The Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity influenced the…
outcome: The Black is Beautiful movement’s rejection of cultural assimilation laid a foundation for multicultural and ethnic studies movements in the future.

topic: Topic 4.12: Black Is Beautiful and Afrocentricity
subtopic: The Black is Beautiful movement and Afrocentricity influenced the…
outcome: Although Afrocentricity celebrates Africa and elevates it to a central position in the identities and histories of people of African descent, it blurs distinctions across ethnicities within the African diaspora. Critics also emphasize the problems of such an approach, including that Afrocentricity can be a substitute for, rather than a challenge to, Eurocentrism.

topic: Topic 4.13: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
subtopic: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
outcome: Explain how the Black feminist movement of the twentieth century drew inspiration from earlier Black women’s activism.

topic: Topic 4.13: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
subtopic: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
outcome: Throughout United States history, Black women played central roles in the struggles for freedom and racial and gender equality. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, activists such as Jarena Lee, Sojourner Truth, and Harriet Tubman resisted injustice and oppression as enslaved and free people. In the 1970s, the Black feminist movement drew inspiration from these Black women activists and others who highlighted Black women’s unique experiences of racism and sexism.

topic: Topic 4.13: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
subtopic: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
outcome: Taking their name from Harriet Tubman’s famous Combahee River raid that freed over 700 African Americans during the Civil War, the Combahee River Collective was a Boston-based, Black feminist and lesbian organization. Their Collective Statement (1977) argued that Black women’s liberation would free all members of society as it would require the destruction of all systems of oppression (e.g., racism, sexism, classism, homophobia).

topic: Topic 4.13: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
subtopic: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
outcome: In the 1980s, writer Alice Walker coined the term “womanist,” which builds upon earlier forms of Black women’s activism through opposition to racism in the feminist community and sexism in Black communities.

topic: Topic 4.13: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
subtopic: The Black Feminist Movement, Womanism, and Intersectionality
outcome: In the 1990s, scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced the term “intersectionality,” which is a framework for understanding the distinct experiences of Black women through the interactions of their social, economic, and political identities with systems of inequality and privilege. The concept of “intersectionality” connected Black feminist scholarship with earlier Black women’s activism.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: Describe the concept of “interlocking systems of oppression” and its connection to earlier Black feminist activism.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: The concept of “interlocking systems of oppression” describes how social categories (e.g., race, gender, class, sexuality, ability) are interconnected, and considers how their interaction with social systems creates unequal outcomes for individuals. The concept examines interrelated contexts, systems, and institutions that facilitate oppression or privilege in many areas of society, including education, health, housing, incarceration, and wealth gaps.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: The concept of “interlocking systems of oppression,” first articulated by Patricia Hill Collins and commonly used in sociology, builds on a long tradition of Black feminist scholars, activists, and writers who critiqued the tendency to treat race, gender, class, and sexuality as mutually exclusive categories.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: Explain how Black writers have represented interlocking systems of oppression in their work.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: Writers like Gwendolyn Brooks and Audre Lorde explore the lived experiences of Black women and men and show how their race, gender, and social class can affect how they are perceived, their roles, and their economic opportunities.

topic: Topic 4.14: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
subtopic: Interlocking Systems of Oppression
outcome: In literature like Maud Martha, writers like Gwendolyn Brooks depict how African Americans negotiate the multiple dimensions of their identity and social class as they navigate spaces within and beyond their communities.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Explain how economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and promoted in the second half of the twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Despite the growth of the Black middle class, substantial disparities in wealth along racial lines remain. Discrimination and racial disparities in housing and employment in the early twentieth century limited Black communities’ accumulation of generational wealth in the second half of the twentieth century. In 2016, the median wealth for Black families was $17,150 compared to $171,000 for white families.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Desegregation in the 1950s and 1960s expanded educational opportunities and gradually increased the number of Black college graduates. By 2019, 23 percent of African American adults had earned a bachelor’s degree or higher.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Urbanization increased opportunities for employment and the growth of Black businesses. Black entrepreneurs have long contributed to American society and the economy. Black-owned businesses, such as restaurants, banks, and publishing houses, were established to serve Black communities; some of these are still in operation today.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Explain how the Voting Rights Act of 1965 impacted the growth of Black political representation in American politics in the late twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 prohibits local and state governments from enacting laws and procedures that create racial discrimination in voting. As a result of the Voting Rights Act, Black voting power and political representation expanded in the late twentieth century alongside the growth of the Black middle class. Many African Americans achieved influential positions as members of Congress, local legislators, judges, and high-ranking officials in presidential administrations.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Economic growth in Black communities has been hindered and…
outcome: Between 1970 and 2006, the number of Black elected officials in the United States grew from about 1,500 to 9,000 officials—a sixfold increase. The largest annual increase occurred in 1971, reflecting the impact of the Black Freedom movement on Black political representation.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Major advances in Black federal political leadership in the…
outcome: Describe major advances in Black federal political leadership in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Major advances in Black federal political leadership in the…
outcome: Shirley Chisholm, an advocate for women’s rights, became the first Black woman elected to Congress in 1968. In 1971, she helped found the Congressional Black Caucus, a group of Black members of Congress that promotes the growth of Black political power by supporting Black candidates in national, state, and local elections, and lobbying for reforms in healthcare, employment, and social service programs.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Major advances in Black federal political leadership in the…
outcome: In 2001, Colin Powell became the first Black secretary of state, serving under President George W. Bush. He was succeeded as secretary of state by Condoleezza Rice—the first Black woman to hold the position.

topic: Topic 4.15: Economic Growth and Black Political Representation
subtopic: Major advances in Black federal political leadership in the…
outcome: The early twenty-first century saw historic precedents in Black executive branch political leadership, with the elections of Barack Obama as president (2008) and Kamala Harris as vice president (2020). They are the first Black Americans to hold these positions in United States history.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: The African American population has grown and become more…
outcome: Describe ways the African American population has grown and become more diverse since 2000.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: The African American population has grown and become more…
outcome: Since 2000, the number of Black college degree holders has more than doubled.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: The African American population has grown and become more…
outcome: The number of Black immigrants in the United States has nearly doubled since 2000, driven primarily by immigrants from Africa and the Caribbean. As the Black population in the United States grows, the number of its members who identify as Black and Hispanic, or otherwise multiracial has also grown.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: The African American population has grown and become more…
outcome: Between 2000 and 2019, the Blackidentifying population in the United States grew by 30 percent to approximately 47 million people, nearly 14 percent of the United States population.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: The African American population has grown and become more…
outcome: The unifying term “Black” indicates a community’s shared African heritage and shared experiences. Black communities in the United States include people with diverse ancestries, histories, and cultures, including the descendants of those enslaved in the United States (who may use the ethnonym “African American”), recently arrived immigrants (who may identify by their race and nationality (e.g., “Afro-Colombian”), and people who identify as multiracial (e.g., with significant Black and white or other ancestry).

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: Religion and faith have played dynamic social, educational, and…
outcome: Explain how religion and faith have played dynamic social, educational, and communitybuilding roles in African American communities.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: Religion and faith have played dynamic social, educational, and…
outcome: In the early twenty-first century, two-thirds of African American adults identify as Protestant, while 20 percent do not affiliate with any religion.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: Religion and faith have played dynamic social, educational, and…
outcome: Black religious leaders and faith communities have played substantial roles in Black civil rights and social justice advocacy by mobilizing their congregations to act on political and social issues, including issues beyond those that directly affect Black communities.

topic: Topic 4.16: Demographic and Religious Diversity in Contemporary Black Communities
subtopic: Religion and faith have played dynamic social, educational, and…
outcome: The Black church has served as an institutional home for developing and debating core values within Black communities related to education, community improvement, race relations, cultural practices, vernacular, and the broader African diaspora.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: Describe ways African American music blends musical and performative traditions from Africa.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: Since their ancestors’ first arrival in the Americas, African Americans have drawn from African-based musical and performative elements as the foundation for the sounds, expressions, and interpretations developed in African American music. These elements include improvisation, call and response, syncopation, storytelling, and the fusion of music with dance.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: Describe the influence of the African American musical tradition on American and global music genres.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: The African American musical tradition, comprised of genres including spirituals, blues, jazz, gospel, rhythm and blues (R&B), and hip-hop, has influenced and revolutionized American (such as rock and roll) and international musical genres (such as Latin jazz).

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: African American performers, such as Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Bo Diddley, and Little Richard, laid the foundation for rock and roll by modifying gospel and blues with new rhythms and electric instruments.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: African American music blends musical and performative traditions from…
outcome: African American music reflects lived experiences of joy, hope, creativity, and social critique in the midst of ongoing racism and oppression.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Describe the origins and elements that define hip-hop culture.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Hip-hop refers to a culture born out of collaboration and artistic creativity among young Black and Latino community members in the 1970s. Rooted in New York City’s Bronx borough, hip-hop has developed into a global phenomenon.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Music is the most enduring component of hip-hop. African American artists like James Brown influenced DJs and the music they shared at community events in the 1970s. DJs like Grandmaster Flash added improvised vocal rhymes and experimented with turntable techniques (e.g., mixing and scratching), which became the origins of modern rap music.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: DJs developed new techniques such as extending the point in a song referred to as “the break.” This provided dancers with extended opportunities to showcase new moves and routines. “Breakdancing” was performed independently by “b-boys” and “b-girls” and in groups (crews).

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Graffiti art predates the facets of music and dance but became another vital form of artistic expression in the emerging youth culture of hip-hop. “Writers,” as they were known, emblazoned walls, bridges, and subway cars with art that brought acclaim to artists like Jean-Michel Basquiat.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Explain how African American political and cultural movements of the 1960s and 1970s influenced the emergence of hip-hop.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: Hip-hop emerged in the wake of the Black Freedom movements and Black Arts movement of the 1960s and 1970s. It blended elements such as Black Panthers’ and Afrocentric fashion, Black nationalism, jazz, and poetry to articulate uniquely African American experiences and identities.

topic: Topic 4.17: The Evolution of African American Music: From Spirituals to Hip-Hop
subtopic: Origins and elements that define hip-hop culture
outcome: After the decline of the Black Power movement, hip-hop vocalized African Americans’ ongoing political struggles and reflected on the state of Black America in the past, present, and future. A wide range of hip-hop artists, from Queen Latifah to Kendrick Lamar, increase awareness of African Americans’ political issues in music that reaches global audiences.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: Describe representations of African Americans on the stage and screen by African Americans in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: To combat the prevalent and racist depictions of African Americans in early twentieth century cinema, filmmakers like Oscar Micheaux presented Black life and characters as realistic and complex. Micheaux produced nearly 50 films between the 1920s and 1940s. He created opportunities for all- Black casts to perform a range of roles that challenged negative stereotypes and paved the way for future Black directors and producers in television and film.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: Soul Train was a popular African American dance program modeled on American Bandstand. The show was created by Don Cornelius in 1971.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: Explain how migration and economic growth influenced representations of African Americans in television and film.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: Black theater in the twentieth century blossomed with companies emerging in urban centers where migrants settled during the Great Migration. Professional and community theaters produced plays tackling political and social issues pertinent to Black life as well as offering depictions of Black joy in both dramatic and musical forms.

topic: Topic 4.18: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
subtopic: Black Life in Theater, TV, and Film
outcome: Since the 1970s, African Americans and African American life have been depicted in ways that attempt to capture the diversity within the culture. Television shows like The Jeffersons (1975–1985) and The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air (1990–1996) portrayed upward mobility; strong family units are characteristic of series such as Good Times (1974–1979) and Black-ish (2014–2022).

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: Contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth…
outcome: Describe the contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth century and beyond.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: Contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth…
outcome: Beginning in Reconstruction, African American athletes demonstrated their abilities and broke barriers in racially segregated sports throughout the nineteenth century. For example, Oliver Lewis won the inaugural Kentucky Derby in 1875; two years later William “Billy” Walker also won the Derby. Lewis and Walker set a precedent that most winners of the Derby would be African American until the early twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: Contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth…
outcome: In 1895, Black athletes in Halifax, Nova Scotia, founded the Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes, which predated the National Hockey League. They established teams throughout the Maritime provinces of Canada.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: Contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth…
outcome: Due to racial segregation in sports, African American athletes created their own athletic leagues. Immediately after the Civil War, African Americans founded baseball associations throughout the country known as “Negro leagues” that persisted until the 1960s. In 1947, Jackie Robinson became the first Black player in Major League Baseball.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: Contributions of Black athletes to sports in the nineteenth…
outcome: African American Olympians have earned many gold medals for the United States. Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Olympics and returned home to racial discrimination.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries…
outcome: Explain how African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries have contested discrimination and advocated for racial equality.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries…
outcome: Through their achievements in many different sports, African American athletes have broken and continue to break racial barriers in sports and used their public platform to promote racial equality.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries…
outcome: In 1967, boxer Muhammad Ali refused to enlist in the United States Army and participate in the Vietnam War. Ali cited religious reasons for his refusal but also pointed out the continued racism at home, stating, “The real enemy of my people is right here.”

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries…
outcome: Olympians Tommie Smith and John Carlos participated in nonviolent protest against racial discrimination when they raised the Black power fist to show solidarity with the Black Freedom movement.

topic: Topic 4.19: African Americans and Sports
subtopic: African American athletes in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries…
outcome: Frustrated by the prevalence of police brutality, in 2016 Colin Kaepernick and other NFL players began kneeling during the playing of the national anthem. This peaceful protest inspired athletes in other sports to do the same, bringing the problem of police brutality into the national spotlight.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: Describe African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: African American inventions and scientific discoveries have had a global impact, with significant contributions in the fields of agriculture, technology, medicine, science, and engineering. For example, George Washington Carver, born enslaved, became a botanist and professor who developed methods for preventing soil depletion and served as a counselor on agriculture to President Theodore Roosevelt.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: African American women like Katherine Johnson and Mae Jemison played instrumental roles in the United States aeronautics and space programs. Katherine Johnson, a mathematician, worked for NASA. Her successful calculations for space travel helped launch astronauts to the moon and back. Physician, engineer, and NASA astronaut Mae Jemison became the first African American woman to travel in space in 1992.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: Describe African Americans’ contributions to American medical care, training, and medical advancements.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: African Americans have contributed in key ways to the American healthcare system, including providing free community-based care that encouraged early diagnosis of illness. African American physicians collaborated with local governments to establish America’s first nonsegregated hospitals in the late nineteenth century and during the Black hospital movement in the mid-twentieth century.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: African Americans established medical schools (e.g., at Meharry College, Howard University, Morehouse, and other HBCUs) and the National Medical Association to support training for Black medical professionals, as they were initially barred from entry into the American Medical Association.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: African Americans’ contributions to scientific or technological advancements
outcome: African Americans have long contributed to advancements in medicine. Among many examples, contributions include the work of Onesimus, an enslaved man who brought awareness of variolation to the British American colonies, which helped curtail smallpox; Daniel Hale Williams, who founded Provident Hospital in Chicago (1891), the first Black-owned hospital in the United States, and performed the world’s first successful heart surgery, in 1893; and Kizzmekia Corbett, who was central to the development of the Moderna Covid-19 mRNA vaccine.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: Multiple, compounding forms of discrimination against Black people with…
outcome: Describe multiple, compounding forms of discrimination against Black people with disabilities as well as governmental responses.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: Multiple, compounding forms of discrimination against Black people with…
outcome: During the early twentieth century, the rise of eugenics heightened the stigmatization of persons considered inferior based on their race and ability. As a result of these stigmatizations, Black people with disabilities encountered multiple forms of systemic oppression, harassment, institutionalization, and infringement of their rights, such as forced sterilization.

topic: Topic 4.20: Science, Medicine, and Technology in Black Communities
subtopic: Multiple, compounding forms of discrimination against Black people with…
outcome: In 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) built upon the civil rights legislative achievements that outlawed Jim Crow by prohibiting discrimination for those with disabilities in areas including housing, employment, and government programs.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: Explain how the discipline of African American Studies has contributed to interdisciplinary academic studies.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: African American Studies remains a primary means to examine the global influence of Black expression and racial inequities. The field analyzes Black history, literature, politics, and other subjects not included in more traditional disciplines, using approaches that focus on past and present Black experiences. These approaches continue to develop as the discipline evolves.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: Explain how Afrofuturism envisions Black lives in futuristic environments.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: Afrofuturism is a movement that reimagines Black pasts, such as a past without oppression, and envisions Afrocentric futures using technology and science. This boundless exploration of new possibilities for Black people comes to life in the intersections of art, music, film, fashion, literature, and architecture.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: Early examples of Afrofuturism include the poet Phillis Wheatley’s visions of future freedom and mobility after abolition, and the mathematician and astronomer Benjamin Banneker’s study of the stars in his Almanac and Ephemeris.

topic: Topic 4.21: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
subtopic: Black Studies, Black Futures, and Afrofuturism
outcome: Afrofuturism’s characteristic works emerged from the 1970s onward, including the music of Sun-Ra and films like Black Panther.
